utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this time of the day, a very good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Vasic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasic. Please be seated. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When the Court rose yesterday, Mr. Vasic, I wanted to take you back to 19 in the Prosecution bundle. Would you have document 19 in front of you, which is the letter from Bishop Komarica. Now, when you were giving your evidence, you were shown this document and you began to say that after receiving this letter you had a meeting with the bishop; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a meeting with the bishop, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would help if I was on the right channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What passed between you and the bishop at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting took place at the bishop's office in Banja Luka, and I got a very nice reception and we met for about an hour. We talked about general matters, and more specifically, we discussed the need for the protection of religious buildings. And the bishop was giving advice and he also asked me to protect minorities in Prnjavor. So basically it was a rather general conversation, and there was just this specific reference to the need to protect the minorities in Prnjavor who had lived there for hundreds of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present, and the bishop, and one of the people working for the bishop; I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How long after the receipt of this letter did the meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but not much later. We spoke on the phone and we agreed to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you say to the bishop about the allegations that he made in that letter of the 3rd of August?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reference to any specific events as such. It was just a general discussion on the need to protect national minorities amongst the others, Croats, who were living in Prnjavor and there were just two per cent of them. Before the war, there were just two per cent Croats in Prnjavor, and there still are today. We discussed the destruction, I believe, the destruction of the Ukrainian church, and I can't remember whether we talked about this attempt to destroy the Croat church, but it was prevented by our police force. And I told the bishop that the people who tried to destroy the Croat church had been dealt with and actually they were handed over to the military authorities, because they were military staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think you told us about that both in your evidence in chief and also cross-examination. And what about this allegation in the letter that involves the Greek Catholic church in Prnjavor? What was said about that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing much to say, because the Ukrainian church had been destroyed. There are two Ukrainian churches in the municipality of Prnjavor. One, as we call it, is Roman Catholic, and the other Greek Catholic. But basically, sometimes the second one is also referred to as an Orthodox Ukrainian church, and the other one Unionist Ukrainian church. A hundred years ago, the Ukrainians came to the municipality of Prnjavor. Some of them embraced Catholicism and there were the Unionists, and the others didn't, so they remained Orthodox. And that's why it's called Greek Catholic. The Greek Catholic was destroyed and the Roman Catholic was not destroyed. And I said earlier that one woman recognised one of the perpetrators when we started investigating the attempt to destroy the second Ukrainian church. And the perpetrators were not originally from Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you meet the bishop on any other occasion, other than the one -- or after the one that you have just told us about?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we met at a larger meeting, and perhaps we talked briefly for five minutes after the war. There was a reception, I think, with the president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to tab 8, please. Now, Mr. Vasic, so far as this report is concerned, had you ever seen it before yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These reports were never submitted to the official bodies or institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Had you seen reports like this, in other words, intelligence-based reports by people with pseudonyms, did they ever get to your level, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Those were unknown individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By looking at this report, are you able to help us at all as to which branch of government, police force, municipality, whatever, in the former Yugoslavia would have produced this?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sort of report can only be drafted by some security service, either a military service or a police service. There were special services within the army and the police who did these things. Back then, those were secret services, in fact, and I have no idea who they were accountable to. And today, these kinds of services are accountable to the Assembly of the Republic, of course, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, looking at the page that is headed "2," on the third line down, the second line of the paragraph, we see two different typefaces. The second typeface begins with the word "Je." Perhaps you'd read those two words with the different typeface, please, and no doubt they'll be translated when you do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness read it again, please, a bit more than one word.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Those are -- I don't know whether you get -- you probably don't hear what the interpreter says. The interpreter has just said, Mr. Vasic, that those two words aren't enough, but what I'm saying is they are the only two words in that typeface, aren't they? That's a question to you, Mr. Vasic. They are the only two words with that particular typeface; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So could you read them again, and I can only ask the interpreter to do their best. If it's really not possible, with the learned Judges' leave, because you'd just say. Read them again, please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Is thoughtless" or "thoughtlessness."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to give any explanation, Mr. Vasic, as to why they are a different typeface?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose something else must have been written here and then deleted, and something was typed over the original text. Perhaps it could be easier to understand within context of a whole sentence, that is. But why this bit has been deleted, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think, in fairness, perhaps you would read the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "SDS got the majority power and it is led by the most extremist streak of the Serb people, and its thoughtlessness led to grief for most management posts held by people of Serb nationalities, and they were blamed for having belonged to the League of Communists and other leftist powers."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had a conversation of sorts, but not in these terms, with Mr. Tieger yesterday, but I would invite the Prosecution to consider whether it is possible for the original of this document to be produced, because I wish to pursue this line of questioning, particularly bearing in mind exactly the point that -- the typeface that has been changed, in other words, the pointed in the document that has been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly not going to be possible at the moment, Your Honour, given the hour, but we'll make every attempt to produce the document or the original document that was seized, whether or not that's the -- an original is another story, as soon as possible, which I presume will be shortly after 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, and I'm not sure I would need to pursue it with the witness, bearing in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see whether there's any issue of authenticity or changes in the document at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's one passage I'd like to take you to, and that is the top of page 3, which deals with the SDA.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you read out the first sentence only, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "SDA, the leadership of this party is under the powerful influence of Islamic fundamentalism. Its cadres are Fuad Klokic, a political scientist, a Marxist, one-time member of Maspok, it's highly unpredictable, and his nickname is Fuad Lagara, the liar. Husein Vukovic, four years of school."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Stop there. Particularly, I'd like you to go to the beginning of the second paragraph that relates to the SDA, that begins with the word "rukovodstva."

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Leadership of this party is very close to Odobasic Jasmin, legal officer from SDP, Muharem Halilovic, until recently chief of SUP, Zehra Halilovic, until recently President of the Prnjavor Municipal Assembly, and Muhamed Klokic, agronomist and the agricultural cooperative director."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you talked about Mr. Odobasic in the course of your evidence, at least in chief. He was in the SDP rather than the SDA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any understanding of what Clara means when he or she says that Mr. Odobasic was close, I think very close, to the leadership of the party, clearly referring to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably what is meant is that he was one of the more extreme Muslims, especially at the time when the SDA party was being set up. All those who came from Sarajevo first came to see him. And I know of a number of people from that leadership who went to Lisnja, to the founding assembly of the SDA together with him. Afterwards, he became president of the exchange committee and he showed his true face because more than a hundred people killed by Mujahedin in Prnjavor he didn't want to help them be exchanged. Only about 15 people who had already been put on the list by the International Red Cross, even though back then we did get in touch with him and we asked him to help us out. But all those who were exchanged were exchanged dead. And two were never exchanged and we got two bodies with heads missing. And he was the president of this committee which has supposed to help out in these exchanges, and I suppose he's the only person who is still afraid to come back to Prnjavor today, because he's afraid of the families of the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like us to come back to the actions of this armed group, the ones we have called the Wolves. Let's talk about their commander. It was Mr. Veljko Milankovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that this man was from the same local commune, from the same area.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the municipality of Prnjavor, from a village there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at some point it was said that he was an entrepreneur, a businessman.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was a criminal before the war, but he was a hero during the war and he was killed in the war in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but before the war, before he created that group of men, of armed men, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had never been any sort of businessman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following: You stated that at some point these men and this man we just mentioned, were walking around in town carrying weapons and that they were threatening the population, both the Muslim and the other population.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the other 2.000 soldiers as well who were walking around fully armed, what I meant was that anyone would be afraid of a person bearing arms. But they were more disciplined than other soldiers. It was a rather disciplined unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you stated that these men were drunk at night, they were carrying weapons, and people were afraid of them. Please, can you explain the following to me: Why did the civilian authorities of the municipality, and you were the president of the said municipality, why didn't you react? Why didn't you make sure that these people were arrested?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was a much more powerful force than the police or the civilian authorities. Everything we could do was to kindly asked them not to carry arms. There were some arrests on the part of the military police, some requests for certain arrests. There have been quite a few of such individual incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you yourself, what measures did you implement in order to protect the civilian population against the acts committed by these men?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything we could do. I mean, we asked the military to deal with these people when such incidents happened. These were individual, isolated incidents. It wasn't a constant practice. There was an order in one of the decisions that I had read out whereby General Talic issued an order according to which military police was no longer allowed to operate in town, but only on the front lines, and that it was up to the civilian police force to deal with the situation in town. So it was just one of the measures I had managed to negotiate with the military authorities, because there had been quite a few complaints about the military police breaking into people's flats, and so that was when the decision was made on the part of the general to ban them from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why could the civilian police not do anything? Why couldn't they intervene?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts, and that's why there was once a conflict between the army and the police force that we had talked about earlier on, when the chief of police was replaced. We asked them to do so, but they had no actual power, because they had only 50 active police officers and then maybe about -- between 50 and 100 reserve officers. And there were at least 2.000 soldiers on leave, fully armed, at any given time. Quite a few of them, of course, were scattered around the villages. They were not all of them in town, but they used to come into town all the time and it was common practice for them to always walk around fully armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you stated very clearly that you disagreed with these acts, but did you write any reports? Did you send any reports to the civilian authorities? I don't know what authorities. Maybe the regional authorities or at the state level. Did you write to anyone to tell them what was going on? Did you write reports to the command of the military in order to say that what these men were doing was completely intolerable for you, as the mayor of this commune, of this community?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Complaints were made, both in writing and orally. And one of the things that they said that we were against was one of the decisions on the part of the Crisis Staff, whereby we wrote a letter to the Crisis Staff of Krajina and we said that we had information that some people within the Crisis Staff of Krajina were working on the formation of the armed forces outside the scope of the regular army and that we wanted an investigation into that. So we wanted to put a stop to the creation of these paramilitary forces and that is referred to in one of the decisions of the Crisis Staff which is in this set of documents. And it was in fact delivered to the Crisis Staff of the Krajina, where there was the headquarters of the police force and the 1st Corps. And I had many other contacts and phone conversations, et cetera. And also, the phone call to President Karadzic asking him to intervene with the army and asked them to tell their soldiers not to carry weapons around when they were on leave. And there were quite a few requests made to the chief of police or -- and the police force in general or the military to intervene with regard to individual incidents. The basic practice was, for example, if there was a problem being created by soldiers in town, we would normally know what unit they came from and then we would call the commander to send the military police from that unit to deal with these men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second point I'd like to discuss with you, I'd like you to clarify, has to do with a topic we dealt with yesterday, the fact that a number of managers were forced to resign. Do you remember that point? And the Prosecutors produced a number of documents where we could see the decisions, the decisions pertaining to these resignations were signed by yourself. And you stated, and I hope that I'm not mistaken in that, you stated that of course a number of people were forced to resign, but what you said is that most people were given other jobs, in other functions, functions that existed at the time of war. So, in other words, these were just formal movements within the employment structure. These people were not deprived of their employment, but they were appointed to other positions, positions that existed only during the war. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you've understood a part of what I've said. All the people were fired because such was the order that was received, and in case of the immediate danger of war, then all the, for example, managers stopped being managers of a particular business, but they became managers in a war situation. And the SDA, that was part of the coalition, then protested because some part of their managers were simply fired or replaced by some other people, and three of them were not Serbs. But I believe that there were two or three managers that came from the SDA, and their replacements were not found for them. Some people who were officers were sent to the front. They were mostly Serbs. They were mobilised. And some other people were appointed in the interim period to perform those duties. For example, the commander of a particular unit was sent to the war, in the military, and then somebody else took his place, and when that person came back from the war, he became director of a technical school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, practically speaking, all these people were appointed to other functions, functions that existed because it was the war. That's what you are telling me. Except for three people who, according to you, were members of the SDA and were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were candidates from the SDA in order to become managers. One of them was the chairman of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were all these people given another job except for three people, who were SDA candidates?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except for those that went to the army, because they accepted to go to the army. But most of the people that went were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. officers, because what we tried to do, ordinary soldiers who -- or rather, the managers who were just soldiers, we thought they should not go to the war because we needed those people. We only sent those people who were officers, and those who were not were kept on their original post, because they were more needed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to force you to do something that might be a bit tedious, but what I would like us to do is to go back to this document that -- with all the decisions. What is the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's 33. We could provide that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Of course, we are not going to run through all the decisions. I don't want to ask too much. But without going through all the decisions, I would like you to point out the cases of people who were forced to resign but who were also given another position, that you described as a wartime position. You were the one who signed all these decisions, so I'm sure you are perfectly aware of what happened to these people later on, so it should be very easy for you to give us some examples of what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not sign any of these decisions. It was the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly who took those decisions. These decisions were taken by the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly, and I didn't sign any one of them, but I knew of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, perhaps I just consulted with Judge Hanoteau. Perhaps we could take a few examples. If you would look at decision number 72, where Mr. Kostresevic seems to be relieved of his duties. That is Mr. Luka Kostresevic. And in decision 123, it seems that he is appointed, whereas in 72 he is relieved from his duties as the director of the public utility company Park Prnjavor [phoen]. In 123, he is appointed director of the public utility company Park Prnjavor. So is that one of the examples of what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first manager, my first manager, and he was later appointed the manager of the public -- yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity, of Mr. Kostresevic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now let's move on to 74, Mr. Krivinskij. Mr. Krivinskij is relieved from his duties as the director of the mixed company Vetprodukt in Prnjavor. And then in 124, we see him reappear as the director of the mixed company Vetprodukt Prnjavor. That's another example, I take it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the ethnicity of Mr. Krivinskij?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he came from a mixed marriage, from a Croat and a Ukrainian, or maybe he's purely a Croat, but certainly he's not a Serb. None of his parents were Serbs and he wasn't a Serb either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would look at decisions 76 and 126, Vrhovac. Could you tell us what the ethnicity of Mr. Vrhovac was?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we look at 77 and 127, Brkovic, what's the ethnicity of Mr. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please read out his first name as well, because there are two Brkovics. One is Pero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check whether I did not mix them up. But in 77 it's Milenko Brkovic who is --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Brkovic was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Milenko Vrhovac is?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A Serb. Let me just have a look at 126, whether I did not mix up any first names. No, it's both Milenko. Then 78, Ignjatic, 128, one relieving Mr. Ignjatic from his duties and 128 appointing Mr. Ignjatic. What was the ethnicity of Mr. Ignjatic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to give me any example of a Muslim being relieved from his duties and reappointed in a similar way. Because we see that decisions to relieve persons from their duties range from decision 68 until 108. That's 40 decisions, apart from some numbering problems, but approximately 40. And then we see that other people are appointed again, and I'm just limiting myself at this moment to the -- well, let's say the economic functions. Then we find from 109 until 152 the appointments, some 43. So that is a number, more or less, balanced. Could you give me an example of a Muslim being relieved from his duties and then being reappointed. And perhaps I've written down at least the first 12 names, so if that would assist you, either Mr. Debeljak, Jevtic, Planicic, Mr. Rupa, Mr. Miljencic [phoen], Mr. Sljivic, Mr. Klokic. So any of these persons being Muslim and being reappointed immediately after relieved from their duties, as we saw it with some Serbs and some people from mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It functioned with Serbs and Croats, and I think that before the war there were only three managers who were of Muslim ethnicity. Otherwise, they were less represented between the managers. I think that Softic Edhem was appointed later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take them. The three Muslim managers, who were they? Could you give us their names? I think you gave one. Yes?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fuad Klokic was a manager of the restoration company, and the chairman of the SDA. He was later on replaced by somebody else when he -- when they went after the coalition and he was not reappointed later on. And Softic Edhem, who was the manager of the veterinary station, he was relieved of his duties and later on reappointed. And he was one of the members of the local parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he reappointed? Was this in this series of decisions? Because these decisions very much concentrate on late May/early June 1992. Could you tell us about Mr. Klokic. So he left. He was not reappointed. Then Mr. Edhem, he was relieved from his duties, when is there a decision? Is it in this range?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was reappointed, but I don't know whether it is written down here. And there is to a Pavle as well, he was not reappointed, although he was a Serb. I've just come across that line here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So from the few --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksandar Krivinskij, Pavle Stula, they were both reappointed, although they were not Serbs. Let me just look it up for a minute here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not generally talking about non-Serbs. You could deal with that, but at this moment I'm looking for Muslims. And I'm trying to -- you say Mr. Klokic was one, he was not reappointed.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have just found it. This is the decision on appointment of a manager in the war conditions, Softic Edhem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What number? Could you give me the number, so that we ...

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on page 112 in the Serbian language. It's number 142, 142.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 142. Okay. Edhem Softic, the veterinarian, was appointed again. And he was Muslim, you said? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's one of the examples where we have reappointments. And that's now clear to me that -- do you have any recollection of any other Muslim being relieved of his duties and not being reappointed? I see Mr. Edhem was reappointed approximately -- Mr. Edhem Softic was appointed at approximately the same time when he was relieved from his duties.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case with all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see that the decisions are very much concentrated in the same period of time, so this certainly is a clear example of --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that there were only three managers even before the war. Before the war, there were very few managers who were Muslims, because most of them were not qualified enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That clarifies the issue of reappointments of those who were relieved of their duties, at least to some extent. I have a few other questions in this respect as well. I did see in this list of -- could you have a look at decision 61. Yes, that's the relief of a magistrate. Was it within the competence of the Municipal Assembly or the War Presidency to, well, to say it in plain words, to relieve judges from their duties?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a municipal court magistrate, and that was under special authorities, because those type of courts are apart in what they do, apart from the ordinary courts, general courts. And that is something that changes very often. Sometimes they are within the competence of the Municipal Assembly, and that was the case in that particular point in time. And I have already explained before why she was relieved, because she didn't want to deal with certain cases. She would simply put them in the drawer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any examples --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we briefly go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Vasic, were there any other examples of judges being relieved from their duties, the same kind of judges, and what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judges at the courts for misdemeanours, I think we only had one or two. I'm not 100 per cent sure. Because it was a small municipality and judges at the municipal courts for misdemeanours were not very many. And so the decision here is not really explained. But we had no other similar cases at this particular court, and the other court was not within my area of competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said one or two, not many. Is your recollection anything --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we only had one. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one we just referred to in decision 61?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was just this one judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. I would like to draw your attention to another decision and ask some explanation, and that's a document which appears under number 33, but I think it's also already in evidence. That is decision number 44, which says that the citizens of Prnjavor municipality in possession of movable and immovable property - and I'm certain that it is already in evidence, but it's now in this bundle under number 33, in evidence again - that these citizens are called upon to report to the municipal secretariat for economy, and if they do not report within, well, let's say approximately two and a half weeks, that they shall be treated in accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff of the ARK and that the property of such citizens shall be declared the property of the state and placed at the disposal of the municipality of Prnjavor. This is, well, a type of --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to previous legislation and on the basis of a decision made by the ARK Krajina, if a property was deserted, it had to be placed on record and placed under the administration of the state. Because we had some cases where citizens had left and then people were breaking into their homes and stealing stuff. So it all had to be documented. And we've got all the relevant documents about the property being returned. I think about a dozens of tractors had been taken and then they were given back to their rightful owners. Because we placed all the movable property, such as vehicles, tractors, or whatever, from the abandoned homes in a warehouse there at the factory, and we just had to keep these abandoned property under control, and that was in line with the legislation which was in force before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, Mr. Vasic, your testimony now, the language you use in your testimony, is not exactly the same as we find in this decision. Because the decision doesn't say that it should be registered, so in order that the municipality could take care of this property in order to return it. But it says: "The property of such citizens shall be declared the property of the state," which means that it's not the property of the citizen anymore, "and placed at the disposal by the municipality of Prnjavor." So the decision clearly says that it's now property of the state, which is a bit different from what you just said. Now, I'd like to know --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says state property, or rather, that the municipality would be able to dispose of that property. That was in line with pre-war legislation. If this property could not be kept safe, it would be sold on the basis of those regulations and the funds would benefit the municipality. And then after the war people would be compensated; they would get some kind of financial recompense. And this refers to the decision in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give me any document in which it clearly says that any money obtained by selling this property would be kept safely for those who owned that property? I mean, not what happened after the war, but during the war, that there was a regulation saying if a house or an apartment or a tractor is sold which belonged to Mr. X or Y, then the money should be kept from Mr. X and Y for compensation. Could you point us at any clear decision in this respect during the war, not after the war?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was regulated by law, and I'm referring to both pre- and postwar legislation here, both the legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know exactly what specific law and what article of that law. But at any rate, on the basis of that very legislation, everybody was compensated afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, well, whether someone was compensated or whether it was -- or whether such compensation was provided for before the war ended are two different matters. Could I ask you: As far as immovable property is concerned, has it been registered who did not report and who, therefore, lost the property of these immovables? Is there a register on what property became state property?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This terminology, the right to dispose of, to be placed at the disposal, was basically meant to indicate that tractors and any other larger objects would be kept at that factory warehouse or else there would be an auction and they would be sold off and then those funds would be paid back to the previous owners after the war. And as to houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as tractors are concerned, that's not what the decision says. So I invited you to point us at any decision, and you said there must have been some legislation, because money was put apart in order for the --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a law regulating the code of conduct in those cases, and it was complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of a property, of some value - I'm not talking about a spare wheel of a tractor, but I'm talking about real property of some major value, belonging to a non-Serb - where the money was kept for the previous am owner and that he was compensated after the war, spontaneously, so not after difficult proceedings, but -- because you say "we kept that money apart." So could you give us an example of some, again, not minor things, but of some substantial property owned by a non-Serb where the money was kept for him and, well, let's say after 1995, that he didn't have to go to court to get it all back, but just receive it back from the municipality who has kept the money for such a long time for him? Could you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can quote one example. I mean, there were very few such examples. For the most part, the property was kept safe and then returned. In the entire municipality, only 400.000 Deutschmarks, 200.000 euros' worth of that property had to be paid back. So there were not very many of such cases. One particular building had been destroyed and the money was given to the damaged party. That is to say, they didn't actually want any money. They wanted to be given an apartment in lieu of the house that had been destroyed. And so they reached an agreement in that way. But there were very few such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about destruction and compensation from destruction; I'm talking about compensation for appropriation by the state of property left by their owners. And I take it that if a building is --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 200.000 euros is the total worth of that property and all that was paid back very swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is there any registration of those properties that were left and where people did not report? I mean, am I talking in terms of tens of people, hundreds of people? Could you give us an idea of what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it's 70, up to 80 cases, tops. And we've got complete records, and there was a special committee selected by the Executive Committee, and they were in charge of all that. And they recorded all that property. And on the basis of those records, the property was returned afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea on what was the percentage of Serbs not reporting and thus losing their property, and Muslims not reporting and thus losing their property? I mean, what was the percentage of property that became state-owned property because of the -- and I'm especially interested in immovable property.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, those people were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you're talking about 70 to 80 people, would that include immovable property? I mean, would that be 70, 80 families leaving their property and thus losing their property?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just so as for there not to be any misunderstandings, we're talking about people who left and didn't entrust anyone with safekeeping. Because if there was anyone else in charge of a house, say, the house Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would not have been considered as abandoned. We're talking about the people who simply left and never said anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now from this 70 to 80 people who left their immovable property behind, how many of them have returned by now, approximately? I mean, how many are now occupying what is or was their property?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All property was returned. As to whether anyone sold that property afterwards, I don't know. But the law was properly implemented. And I think that more than 90 per cent of them actually had come back. There was no census recently, but I think about 90 per cent of those people came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when you're talking about the law, what law are you referring to, and when was it enacted?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was regulated on the basis of both pre- and postwar legislation, and the constitution of the Serb Republic that provides relevant guarantees as well. I can't remember the exact reference, but it can certainly be found. There is a law and the relevant article, but I can't remember what it is. I think I must have a CD listing all the laws passed by the Assembly of the Serb People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the constitution provisions. I can leave the CD to the Court, if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties are interested to have a look at it. I'm looking at ... Now, another matter. The legal basis for appropriation by the state of that property, what would that be? Because if you do not report within two weeks -- and the decision was taken in times where people might not immediately verify all the decisions taken by the municipality. What was the legal basis for appropriation of this property, apart from this decision? Let me say the following: I would be surprised if I went on a holiday for four weeks and upon my return I would -- of course, I do understand that the situation is different, but I would like to know what is the legal basis for this decision?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal basis is enshrined in law, and I'm quite certain that the secretary who spelt it out in this way actually complied with the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you couldn't identify the law. Most legal systems have an extensive protection for the free enjoyment of property, so therefore, I'm interested to know what kind of law that is. If you don't know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is a law on abandoned property. I think that's the title. But I'm not a legal expert myself, so all this is slightly alien to me. But it is certainly possible to find it on the CD. And those things were put under the protection of the state, as it were, for the sake of protecting that property, and in line with the relevant legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have said that a couple of times. Therefore, I'd like to invite the interpreters to look at, if you have got the bundle, at decision 45 and read to me the -- or at least we'll ask the witness to read the last portion, and I do see that in the translation until now -- let me see. No. It's 44, as a matter of fact. Oh, yes. It's one of the examples where the numbering -- 44. It also means that the translation, the original has a 44, a 45, a 46. However, the translation has a 44 and then jumps to 46. So I'd like you to look at 44, and I invite the Prosecution to come up with a complete translation. I'd like you, Mr. Vasic, perhaps you could assist us to read the portion where it says: "Any failure to report by the above date." That's the second part of the first article. Could you slowly read that, so that it could be translated by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Citizens who by this date do not report will be treated in accordance with a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region, their property shall be declared the property of the state and placed at the disposal of the municipality of Prnjavor. This decision shall not apply to the citizens ..." I think the next sentence is essential as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand that those who were working abroad were not subject to this -- well, of course I read that. I'm mainly interested in those cases where this decision did apply. Again, you have stressed again and again that the property was kept safe by the state, whereas the decision - and that's the reason why I asked the interpreters to again translate it - doesn't say we'll keep it for you, but it says it's now property owned by the state. Could you tell me: When was the compensation and the return of this 70 to 80 left properties which became state property, when was it completed?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. We had individual cases and they were dealt with separately. But all property and ownership legislation was in line with this and it had to do with the return of the citizens as well, those who wished to return, that is. But as we received the requests, as people came along, the cases were dealt with. But the entire procedure was very short. There were no court cases, because nobody complained or appealed any of these decisions. There was just a single case on the part of a Serb whose property had been destroyed and he felt that he had not been given enough money for that, and that was dealt with at a higher level. But everything else was resolved very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was not, or was it, the case you referred to earlier about the destroyed building and compensation for that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That case was settled out of court with the parties involved, so that was not the one I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't give any clear answer. The correspondence we had a look at earlier, as part of the documents you provided to the Defence team of the OSCE, was it in relation to this? Because there was a letter about completing the -- successfully completing the procedures of - what was it exactly? - was that related to -- "fulfilled its obligations under the property laws as outlined in the - I can't read it - substantial completion guidelines." That letter, sent by the deputy representative of the High Representative, is that about completion of this, well, giving back ...

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This referred to everything, generally. This plan for the implementation of property laws arranged by the international community, or the plan for the application of property laws put together by international organisations was implemented according to relevant rules and regulations, and there is a reference to that here. And according to that plan, everything that was encompassed by the plan was processed and then these three organisations checked the documents from the municipality of Prnjavor, and the conclusion was reached that it had essentially been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you give us an indication, because this letter is 2005, so that's at least a long period of time. But could you give us an impression on the first ten immovable property returned and put at the disposal of Muslims? Because you said most of the 70 to 80 were Muslim properties. When was that completed? Could you tell us? 1998, 15 families re-installed in an ownership? Or could you give us an idea on how that happened?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that, as people came along bearing these requests, the requests were processed speedily. Some cases were resolved as early as 1996. I'm quite certain that at least 200 cases were dealt with as early as 1996, and probably more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said 200 cases. Earlier, about immovable property --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say 200. Maybe it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the biggest number of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then that's corrected. You said as early as 1996. Is there any register kept of -- because I'm confronted at this moment with the situation in which during the wartime there is a decision which clearly states it's state property now. You tell us that that was not the case because it was just the property kept in safekeeping by the municipality in order to return it after the war. I asked you about any documentation on this, and you have until now not been able to provide it. And therefore, I'm interested to know exactly what happened with this 70 to 80 cases, mainly Muslims, as you told us, how long it took, whether it was immediately returned. Because I now do understand that upon application, people would get it, and it was a quick procedure. How quick? Two months, six months, one year and a half, three years?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time needed depended on how busy the courts were. I think it was done very quickly. I'm not familiar with all the details, but I'm quite certain that as people came along -- I mean, Your Honour, some people came back in 1998. Some people didn't come back immediately. But when they did come back and lodged their application, they could be entitled to all these things. I mean, we have full records on these returns. I don't have them here, because I didn't think it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that people had to go to court to file an application to be re-installed in their ownership? Is that what I can ...

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the applications were lodged with the municipal secretariat, so not actually the courts, except for this one case of dispute where this one Serb citizen asked for more funds. But they didn't actually have to go to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, you tell us that the speed depended on how busy the courts were. That's what you said one minute ago.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I'm not an expert in that area. You have to understand that. I probably misspoke. What I meant was the authorities in charge of that. I was no longer the president of the municipality, so I'm not familiar with all that. And I'm not a legal expert, so I don't know who was in charge of all that. I think the relevant body was the municipal secretariat, and it was probably their job. I think I must have made a mistake when I referred to courts. It was only -- of course, if anyone contacted the courts, the courts would contact the municipal secretariat as to all these things and how they were dealt with and the procedure, I'm not too familiar with it, but I do know that it was all done according to the procedure enshrined in law. I'm certain of that. And I can also provide the relevant documents as to each individual return, because those documents do exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said it depended on how busy, well, let's say the municipal secretariat was, how long it took. Could you give us an average time? Because I suggested to you whether it was two months or two years. On average.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two months, perhaps. Certainly no longer than two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting on the day on which the relevant party lodged their application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anyone who lost his property who did not report at this moment? Is there any one of this 70 or 80 who never claimed their property back?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever claimed their property had the right to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not an answer to my question. My question was whether anyone did not claim their property back who lost it on the basis of the decision we just discussed. I didn't ask whether they had a right. I asked whether there was anyone who, for whatever reason, refrained from such a claim.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's all registered first, the loss of property, then it should be possible to verify whether all that property which was kept safely for the owners, or the previous owners -- are there registers? Do you know where we could find that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the municipality of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you, but Judge Hanoteau has one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger, I was wondering if you could help me, because I didn't write this down. Could you tell me where one can find the report which you mentioned pertaining to the expulsion of the people, inhabitants of Lisnja. During the cross-examination, you said there was the military report which was confidential, and this report mentioned the expulsion of the inhabitants of Lisnja, and I didn't write this down. I was wondering if you could help me out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd be happy to, Your Honour, if you'd just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps meanwhile, Mr. Josse, I could ask you whether, apart from this last question still to come, whether there would be any need to put further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do have a number which arise from Your Honours' questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do understand that. And I didn't hear any sign of Mr. Krajisnik with additional questions. May I take it that he has none or -- we should have asked earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll check.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's found at tab 12. It's previous Exhibit P892, tab 87 -- tab 12 of the materials presented in Court. It's a report that's headed, after it says "strictly confidential," "1st Krajina Command, with the confidential number 2 June 1992. And I think the reference in Court was to the paragraph enumerated as number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You, Mr. Tieger, also referred to the following: The Muslim population of the [Previous translation continues]... [In English] Expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was a reference to the last sentence of paragraph 2 of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you show this document to the witness, please. Witness, when you were shown this report, you answered by saying that this was a lie. I remember your answer. This is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Prosecutor, during his cross-examination, showed you a document dated on the 3rd of June, 1992, signed by General Talic, where cleansing is mentioned, cleansing of this community, you also said that this was not true. You said that this was a lie. I would like to understand why you claim outright that this is a lie. When you say that it is a lie, you have to be able to prove it. These are official documents. I don't know in which country you were living. Report dated the 2nd of June, 1992. Then there is a document that has been certified by General Talic. So a while ago we mentioned a report drafted by the intelligence services. You said these are people who don't like us. I'm sorry. I think I heard you saying this. You said these were Communists. You can't believe these people, people who have a grudge against us. I'm prepared to believe that these are unidentified intelligence services and these people will not be writing things which are particularly favourable to you, but where we are talking about reports which have been drafted by the military or by a general, and these reports state that there were expulsions, the other report states that there has been ethnic cleansing, and you say that this is a lie. Why do you say that this is a lie? This, I don't think -- I'm sorry, but when you say that this is a lie, I don't think that that is an appropriate answer.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that on the basis of my presence and on the basis of the fact that I saw everything with my own eyes. This report by General Talic was also drafted on the basis of the reports coming from these Claras or whatever they called themselves, these intelligence officers submitting these reports. And what kind of cleansing they had in mind here, I do not know, but I can state upon my full responsibility that I saw with my own eyes, and I said myself that about 30 vehicles involved in this shooting drove in the direction of the main road. And I myself told them and invited them to go back home, and that's what I did. And they all turned back. And that was an activity engaged in by the army and the police. As to my own area of competence, it referred to hunting rifles only, and that is the decision that I myself wrote and signed and handed over to the police. As to all the other reports and the police and army and what sort of reporting this is, I still stand by what I said about those people and their morality and trustworthiness of their documents. They bear no name, no stamp, no nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's all very well, as far as a confidential report is concerned, but of the ARK, but in this case, these are proper, official documents. They bear reference numbers. These come from the command of a particular military corps. These documents bear a date. So are you saying that the military authorities were so unaware that they were prepared to draft reports based on hearsay or anonymous intelligence reports? Do you really believe that a general or a commander in charge of an army can just draft or write anything? Because some intelligence service or more or less clearly identified intelligence service provided some kind of information? Is that what you're saying? Can you go as far as that? Can you actually say that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading this, I just do not understand. It is not clear to me. Because it doesn't say "ethnic cleansing," so this term "cleansing," I don't know what they had in mind. Maybe some environmental operation or what. Or I don't know what the general meant, or the person drawing up this report. I can only talk about the events that I myself witnessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this military report, the -- they quite clearly talk about the expulsion of Muslims. So please answer this question: Will you go as far as saying that the military in that level of command would draft a report based on the mere information provided by some kind of intelligence service? Is that what you're saying, and are you prepared to go as far as that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reports were drafted only and exclusively on the basis of the information provided by their intelligence officers in the field. It was not the general who would have visited the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having a look at the clock and knowing that we have little time available, Mr. Josse, how much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Mr. Tieger, would there be any need, apart from unexpected developments in re-examination, would you need --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I need approximately the same. I'll try to make it less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that would take altogether some 20 minutes. We also need a break. Mr. Registrar, could you inform us as to how far the tape would allow us? Because if we could continue, but I'm also looking at the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik has told me previously he would rather confer with me. And that's not an unreasonable request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, I'll hear about the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I'm addressing the interpreters. 26 minutes left on the tape. That means that either we take a break now of 20, 25 minutes and change the tapes and then continue for another 20 minutes or that we would say that within the next 25 minutes we have to finish. I do see from some hand signs that the interpreters would be willing to continue. Thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour is going to continue? Because I was hoping to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you wanted to -- yes, I'd prefer to continue. If there's any way of resolving that. Because we know that the witness already returned once and we want him to catch his plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just give me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I decided that it would be 14 minutes for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Defence and 12 minutes from the remaining 26, but you're now equal at 12 and 12, because the tape is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you've been asked at some length about population movement back into Prnjavor after the war. That's something you say there are records in existence about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no census of the population, but there are records in the adequate institutions where they have to report once they come back. But this is something regular, when people have to report, when they come or go from -- or cease to be residents in a certain municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You said that records could be provided, if required. Where are these records?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law, in the police stations, people have to report as residents or when they cease to be residents in the municipality of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you provide these records to this Court?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How would you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask the people who work at the municipalities who make photocopies of that for the requirements of this Tribunal, and then I would hand it in to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've been referred by the learned Judge to the letter that you brought here from the Office of the High Representative. That letter talks about property law implementation. What do you understand by the expression "property law implementation"?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Property law implementation, to my mind, is that all those who lodged an application, who asked to get, whether they had a right to get, they got it, and that that process has been completed, according to the standards determined by the international community after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you have that document in front of you from the Office of the High Representative, and also the one from the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission, these are now, clearly, should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The changed role from -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you -- we have two documents, then. The first one being a letter of the 4th of January, 2005, from Ambassador Wnendt to Subotic and Zivkovic, although not one of the clearest -- well, the problem is that we have different versions of it, but the content seems the same. And the second one is the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please. Upon my request, I asked for it to -- I asked it to the municipality, and this gentleman wrote an accompanying letter. This one from 2005. He simply informs that he is sending what was requested. Because I did not ask it from the municipality; I asked it from the Office of the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. I mean, the letter is there, and the other one -- that would have the letter of the 4th of January. We'll later find out which version exactly, because different headings over it. That, Mr. Registrar, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D71, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D71. And then the other one is a document, in the heading it says "organisation for security and cooperation in Europe," and it seems to be addressed to Mr. Zivkovic. There's no translation yet, and signed by Igor Licina. Please proceed. That would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So let me simplify matters. Why did you bring the letter from Mr. -- why did you organise for the letter from Mr. Wnendt to be sent to this Court? What were you hoping to show by bringing it here?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hoping to show by this letter that property was not taken away from the citizens but that it was dealt with according to the law, and that we were trying to get back the property to their owners and that we were the first municipality in Prnjavor to proceed like that, and to prove also that there was rule of law in the municipality of Prnjavor when all that was put under control. I thought that this letter would simply corroborate that. And indirectly, it would help to show that people did return to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My final matter goes back to the issue of Lisnja and what happened to the Muslim population there after the operation. Did all Muslims at that point leave Lisnja or did any return immediately after the military operation?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said on three occasions that there was a group of some 30 vehicles to whom I told to go back, and they all did go back. I do not know whether some people left, those people whose houses had been set on fire. That might have been individual cases that might have happened. But during this particular operation, it did not occur. That is what I saw with my own eyes, and that is what I told those people, and I did see that they did go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's jump forward to today, Mr. Vasic. Lisnja, is the village in existence today?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the village today, please?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Muslim Lisnja, where only the Muslims live.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about the mosque that was destroyed? What's happened to that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All mosques were rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, one moment, please, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is only one thing that I would like to add. According to the rules, they had a right to rebuild the mosques, just as they used to be. And in Prnjavor, they wanted to build a higher mosque, some 13 metres higher. They asked me to ask the head of our municipality to -- and I intervened, and they built a minaret that is 23 metres high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Vasic, I'd just like to be clear on what you're trying to tell the Court about the nature of the reports prepared by General Talic and submitted to the VRS Main Staff. So it's your position that, if I understand it correctly, that General Talic's subordinates in the field had no obligation to inform him about what was happening in their area of responsibility, but all of that was left to unnamed operatives like Clara, to unnamed intelligence operatives, and the subordinates didn't provide any information to their superiors. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Talic appointed a group, a smaller group, that took part in that particular operation, and probably they did not submit any report, but otherwise, General Talic did make some kind of bizarre decisions which are not quite general-like, where he says, "I approve that Zeljko Milanovic can, with his identity papers, only take wherever he wants and whenever he wants armament and rockets." It is simply ridiculous to see something like that. And you can see the general's signature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have limited time. You've taken a position about how reports like this are prepared as if you were either present when those happened or part of that process. And now when I ask you about it, instead of clarifying your position, you return to your criticism of General Talic for the same thing you criticised him for on about three or four occasions during this testimony. Now, I ask you again: Is it your position that General Talic's subordinates had no responsibility to inform him, through reports or otherwise, about what was happening in their area of responsibility, and he was just relying upon information provided by some unnamed intelligence operatives, like Clara?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking into account that this is untrue, then I am claiming that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it seems that the witness has no clear knowledge but draws conclusions from what is in the report and what is in his recollection, and I have not heard one word of real knowledge on how these reports were created. So, therefore, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me return to the issue of dismissals and appointments very quickly. I'm afraid we can't go through it as systematically as I might choose, but I want to ask you about some names that I've had an opportunity to look at and try to check quickly about the terminations and about any appointments. So let me ask you about some names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Document 33, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Muhamed Klokic, what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He was dismissed on May 29th, as far as I can tell. Was he reappointed or not? I don't see any reappointment.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is no evidence of reappointment, then it means that he was not reappointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dervo Jugo, what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see that he was terminated or dismissed on May 29th. I don't see any reappointment. Was he reappointed or not?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But that was a particular company that -- an agriculture company that had various branch offices in various villages. And Jugo Dervo worked there, and the manager was a gentleman by the name of Klokic, who was the brother of the president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Suad Klokic, ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. And he was the brother of the chairman of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see a termination on June 26th, and I see no evidence of a reappointment. Was he reappointed?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me where that was? Because I was not aware that he had been a manager of anything. What number is it here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which reads "Suad Klokic, a lawyer from Prnjavor, is hereby relieved from the duties as director of the Automobile and Motorcycle Club, Stanko Vukasinovic, Prnjavor."

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it. I do note whether that company was really operational. I am not aware of that particular case. Because it was a company where only three people worked, so I do not know whether the company was actually operational. But the four Klokic cases, Klokic was chairman of the SDA, who appointed them for the sake of the coalition with us, and when the coalition split up, that was when they were dismissed. And that's the same thing today, when a coalition fails through [as interpreted], then they appoint other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll just ask you about a couple of other people quickly and then I want to move on to some more general questions. Dzuko Huremovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us the number, perhaps, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have the number handy, but it was on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most of them are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My only question, Mr. Vasic, is: What is Djuka Huremovic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite get the name. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Djuka Huremovic.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was she married to a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Huremovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was she married to a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Jozo Barukcic, was he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Slavko Kalinic, was he also a Croat?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware whether he was a Croat or a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Vera Halilovic Vera or Zehra Halilovic, ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
