utterances.text: Zehra Halilovic was a member of the central committee in the municipality of Prnjavor before the war. She was a Muslim. She was a very extreme wing of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wasn't she the manager of the regional health insurance fund Banja Luka, Prnjavor branch office? I find her in 93. Well, we could continue for some time. Mr. Tieger, I do know that at least we found more than three managers of Muslim ethnicity. Mr. Vasic, I take it that you're aware, or your testimony was clear that there were no more --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was not a manager --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it may have -- at least in the decision relieved from her duties as -- well, we can read the documents, and Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, were Serbs who were members of SDP or otherwise not members of SDS, dismissed but given an opportunity to offer an oath of allegiance to SDS, and were those who declined to do so dismissed and not reappointed?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say that you are mentioning here not only the managers, because many of the names that you read out are not managers. Zehra was not a manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question. I said Mr. Tieger could put the next question to you. You want to add something, we'll see whether there's time for that. Please answer the question of Mr. Tieger whether an oath of allegiance was required from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There were Serbs who were dismissed but reappointed when they offered an oath or pledge of allegiance, and there were Serbs who were dismissed and not reappointed when they declined to do so; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was an agreement between parties about the appointment of a higher manager, and so the parties have got the right, that used to be the case and it is the case, to appoint managerial staff. So Softic Edhem was appointed in the veterinary station, and he was not a member of the SDA. He is a Muslim. But everything was done according to the party line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the witness for one reason or another does not want to answer your question. We have one and a half minute left on the tape. Mr. Tieger, I don't know whether there's any --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have one more question, but I would defer to the Court, if the Court has additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we should finish the examination of the witness. Mr. Vasic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you for having come to The Hague, not only once, but even twice, and I apologise for the inconvenience it may have brought to you. I wish you a safe trip home again and I hope you'll catch your plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid there's something that needs to be dealt with in private session in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we're running out of the tape in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know that. It is quite important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session. Is it about asking the witness. Let's just first turn into private session. It's over. There is no reporting anymore at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For my part, that doesn't matter. It's a formal matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Prosecution would agree, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not being recorded on tape, but we still have the transcribers. You get one minute to explain what you'd like to do. Private session might not be needed because there's no recording anyhow. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We go into private session, but that's rather a paper matter at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you'd just wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is only one thing that I would like to do. I would like to thank you for your understanding. Because this is the first time round in my life that I'm a witness in the court proceedings. So if ever I made a mistake, it was unintentional. Thank you for being so correct and thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We'll adjourn. Let's take a little bit of a longer break. Are you ready to call your next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I want to speak to him briefly, and I mean briefly, but I will do that during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about a break of 40 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- exceptionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Your Honour. I merely wanted to note that we have the original of the document that -- the document that is in the evidence vault requested by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll look at that as well during the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar. We'll adjourn until -- yes, until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, I'd like to explain so that that's on tape now as well, that we failed to have the last few minutes of the previous session on tape; that we dealt with a matter in private session which could have no impact, I would say, on any determination this Chamber will have to make. It was a procedural matter which stands fully alone. Therefore, everything is on the written transcript, but there's a small portion missing on the tape. We decided to continue only because of the urgency of the witness to leave The Hague. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. This being on the record, we started early this morning. I suggest to the parties that we have today one more one-and-a-half-hour session and not have any further breaks, and even if it would be one hour and 35, so that we would finish at approximately close to 1.00 and not resume anymore today. Mr. Josse, that would not disturb any --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Agreeable from my point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also do it because it's a hard task for the interpreters and we -- I take that they would also prefer not to have two short sessions but one longer one and then finish for the day. Yes. Both counsel standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I stood because I thought that Mr. Josse was standing in anticipation of calling the next witness, and I wanted to wrap up some short but lingering procedural matters before we move to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, unless there's any objection against that. I'd rather not at this moment deal already with the exhibits from Mr. Vasic, because I want to have it organised for myself, and it will give an opportunity to the registrar to be well-organised so we can go through it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine. If I can just say for the registrar's benefit that we need numbers for tabs 36 through 39 and for the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar will prepare that on his list so that we can deal with it quickly tomorrow. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we were just about to return the document that had been retrieved from the evidence vault. Mr. Josse has had an opportunity to review it and he does not require it any further. I only bring that to the Court's attention before we replace it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If these were the procedural issues. Mr. Josse, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was Mr. Divcic, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you're invited to escort Mr. Divcic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. I take it that you're Mr. Divcic. Yes. Mr. Divcic, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Divcic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Josse, who is counsel for Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your name, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: My name is Aleksandar Divcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Divcic, I want to begin by asking you a little bit about your own past. When and where were you a student?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo and my entire family had lived in Sarajevo for several hundreds of years. As to my active life, my education, et cetera, all that happened in Sarajevo. I'm a telecommunications engineer, and I had a job in Sarajevo up until the 11th of April, 1992, when I was dismissed because I was a Serb and because of my political commitment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll come to that a little later, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Tieger, would you oppose if Mr. Josse would just lead the witness through his past, which usually saves some time? And I take it that you have at least some idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. In fact, it's really not going to take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Just for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's your involvement in the Communist Party that I would like you to tell the Chamber about, please, Mr. Divcic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and I joined the League of Communists when I was 17 and I was at secondary school. That was the procedure that was put in place in order to attract as many members as possible. So let's say several students would be selected in every class, their names would be put forward, and then they would be invited to join the League of Communists. It was a great honour at the time, and I myself joined the League of Communists because of my deep-seated convictions. I felt that it was a praiseworthy political organisation, so at the age of 17 I joined the Communist League.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when you were at university and your early days of working, were you involved in Communist politics at all?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: For those of you who are not familiar with the environment in the former Yugoslavia, it might be difficult to explain this, but it's a kind of inertia which develops, and then you continue as a member, first of all in secondary school, then at university, in the army, at your place of work. But throughout that time it wasn't an involvement in politics as such, along the lines in which it's done in the West or in the way in which it's being done in my country at the moment. When we had meetings, those were meetings dealing with the practical analysis of the situation at the place where you happen to be, in the army or at your place of work. But it wasn't a political involvement as such, in the true sense of the word. I do apologise. May I just add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I was never a high-ranking party official. I was just a simple member, a grass-root member.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As the communist system collapsed, did you have further involvement in politics?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: There was a kind of political vacuum between the obvious downfall of that sort of system and what was to follow. It was quite obvious that, considering developments in the world as a whole, certain changes would come about in our country and, in Yugoslavia, that there would be a multi-party system, the so-called multi-party system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did your political involvement at that time - and we'll deal with the specific dates in a few moments - but at the time of the collapse of Communism manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Nominally and formally, like everyone else, I was still a member of the Communist League, but there were no meetings and nobody was taking things seriously, as it were. And we were holding our breath, so to say, to see what was going to happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you became involved in informal discussions relating to a different sort of political creed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I socialised with some other people of my age, my friends, that is, and we all felt the need for Bosnia and Herzegovina and Sarajevo, the city in which I lived and worked, to have the same kind of development that was taking place in Belgrade, in Slovenia, and to a certain extent in Zagreb as well. In a way, we always looked upon them as somewhat more advanced areas and places than Sarajevo itself. I don't know if this is an answer to your question. However, more specifically, it was obvious that the communist system was coming down, and us Serbs were afraid of what was to come. We were afraid because we could look back on extremely negative experiences in World War I and World War II, when there were mass killings of Serbs perpetrated by Muslims and Croats, who were organised in Ustasha organisations, that is to say, Nazi formations from Germany. So there was still caution. We feared that history might repeat itself. There were references in the press to the effect that the Muslims were going to get organised, and I'm referring to the early 1990s, the beginning of 1990. There were references to the fact that the Muslims were going to get organised within their own political party and they were asking for that, and the same for Croats. And it was quite obvious what was going on in Croatia in 1990. The Ustasha emigrants were coming back to Croatia, a country that they fled after World War II. So it was a rather tense and unpleasant atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1989, did you attend some informal political meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were informal gatherings of some of us young people who were feeling the need for Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina to set up their own party. Because as Serbs, we felt threatened. And at that time, we had several informal meetings. A friend of mine, a personal friend and myself, were fully aware of the need for setting up such an organisation, but it was quite clear to us that we were not the ones who were likely to be the leaders. We were not all that well known. This friend of mine graduated at the faculty of philosophy. At that time, the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo was considered to be the breeding ground for those who had different opinions. And he got in touch with a professor who, a couple of years earlier, was one of his lecturers, Professor Dr. Aleksa Buha, and he consulted with him, and he came to me and he said to me with a great deal of caution, the professor indicated to him that there was already a like-minded gentleman and that it would be a good idea to go and speak to him. And this man was -- may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I ask the name of this man, the name you referred to, and then we'll go back to the name of the friend who put you in touch with him. So the person you were referred to was whom, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the name of your friend who, via Professor Buha, put you in touch with Radovan Karadzic, is what, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Vojislav "Bato" Kecman. Bato was his nickname, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So when did you first meet Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kecman was the first to go and see Mr. Karadzic. And then he said to me that it would be a good idea for me to go as well. And I was a bit busy, so we couldn't manage it on the same day. I think I went a couple of days later, and I think it must have been February 1990. I visited Dr. Karadzic at his flat. I was given a phone number, and I announced my visit and then I visited the first time. I met the doctor's wife, the then doctor's daughter, and some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was all in Sarajevo. I think it was in February 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like some detail, please, to tell us about this initial meeting with Dr. Karadzic. What was discussed? What happened as a result of it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I had already found some other people. It was a fairly varied group of people, and I'm quite certain that Mr. Vladimir Srebrov was one of them, as well as Mr. Tomo Sipovac. A couple of young men from different faculties and universities. I can't remember their names at the moment, because I never saw them again. And later on, I can't remember whether all that happened in the course of that first visit. But I did visit with him very often. But at any rate, I met Professor Dr. Savo Ceklic, Velibor Ostojic, Ilija Guzina, Professor Aleksa Buha, Rajko Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right, but that doesn't quite answer my question. I was going to come to ask you about some of these other names. The first meeting with Dr. Karadzic, what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Well, quite frankly, those were dangerous times. According to the legislation which was still in place, all of us could have been accused of undermining the constitutional order of the state. And we could have been sent to court. And to a considerable extent, I was listening in to all these conversations in order to assess whether Dr. Karadzic was a serious man, whether all the rest of them were serious and whether they had a serious intention to engage in a very serious task, such as the organisation of a party and the work of a party. My initial impressions in relation to Dr. Karadzic were very positive indeed. And as to some other of the people I've mentioned before, not quite so much. I spent three to four hours there on that first occasion, and then I waited for all the rest of them to leave, and I think Dr. Karadzic and his wife and myself remained alone and we had a serious conversation about everything. I think his wife was simply there in order to make us coffee, et cetera. She didn't take part in this conversation between Dr. Karadzic and myself. And we agreed in our assessment that Serbs had to get politically organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So the people you had named in the answer a minute or two ago, were they all at the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: No, not at the first meeting. I'm absolutely certain that, apart from Dr. Karadzic, Vladimir Srebrov was present at that first meeting with those young lads, then Tomo Sipovac, and I think I must have met the others on subsequent occasions. And these people are people that I still know today, and that's why their names were etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, after that first meeting, other meetings followed; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did those other meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: All those meetings at that period of time were held at Dr. Karadzic's flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how many meetings do you think you attended at Dr. Karadzic's flat?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: About ten. And it went on up until March, the end of March. I know that because for health reasons I had to -- no, maybe the beginning of April. At any rate, I had to go to the coast for health reasons at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is 1990, is it, Mr. Divcic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At what point in time did these discussions develop into an agreement to form a political party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Well, we were actually meeting in order to discuss that. We were all aware of the need, and I think it kind of happened. We simply talked about who was going to be the president of the party and who was going to lead the party. And my impression, if I may -- and basically, my initiative was looking for and spotting somebody who would be dignified, responsible, skilful, capable, a person who would be fit to take over the leadership of this new Serb party, and I myself spotted Dr. Radovan Karadzic. On the occasion of that first visit, when we remained alone, I told him what my impressions were, and on that occasion, I wasn't quite convinced that he liked the idea. I just didn't know for what reason he was telling me that he was not really inclined to take on the leadership. And afterwards, I realised what the reasons were. The events actually indicated why he said what he did, and perhaps I can comment on this a little bit later. But at that stage, he was not in the mood to take on the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party, as it was called afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that leads me to my next question, the name of the party. How was the name of the party chosen or how did it emerge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: In fact, the party had to be democratic, and it had to be a party. By the nature of things, it should have been a democratic party. And what we wanted was for the Serb people to recognise it straight away and to name it, to give it in its title the name "Serb." It was at that time a moment when parties were created which, in their name, had the name of a particular nation. But on the other hand, it was also forbidden at that time, and I can't remember exactly according to what articles of the law, but I know we were walking on a very slippery slope then, and we were deciding on maybe a different name, like the Independent Democratic Party, [B/C/S spoken], and then saying that maybe if the law would change, we would change the name into the Serb Democratic Party. But anyway, we had to abide by the then -- by the laws that were in existence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move back to the issue of the leadership. When was the inaugural meeting of the party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: The inaugural meeting of the party, you are actually asking for the date when the Serb Democratic Party was founded, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, give that answer, and it may not have been what I was intending to ask you, but give that answer and we'll go from there.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, which is St. Peter's Day, which is a Serb Orthodox festival, so it was in Sarajevo, in the hall called Skenderija and I was one of the organisers, which Mr. Karadzic asked me actually to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that -- prior to the meeting, had a decision been made as to who the leader of the party was going to be?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: There was a certain rivalry that existed. I know Mr. Vladimir Srebrov; he was a poet. I think that he also graduated from the faculty of philosophy. Aleksa Buha knew him. Because later on, when they met at one of the meetings in the flat, they greeted one another and they had a discussion and they were slowly antagonistic in their words. Anyway, Mr. Srebrov as far as I know, wanted to become the leader of the Serb Democratic Party, a party which at that time did not have a name. To my mind, it was somebody who would not have been able to do that particular job. And I think that I wouldn't have taken part in that political party under the leadership of that particular man. What I'm aware of, and it is something that I did verify later on, and what I'm telling you is exact, namely, that the leadership of the party was offered to Professor Dr. Nenad Kecmanovic, and that Dr. Karadzic saw himself as the vice chairman. But Dr. Kecmanovic refused to do that, and we forced, quote/unquote, Professor Karadzic to take that particular task upon himself, so he had to do it. We all thought that he was very capable of doing -- of having such a role. And many people amongst us said: If you will not take that role, we will not be a part of it. Certainly, I was one of those people who said that. At that meeting, where I was and Dr. Karadzic was, Aleksa Buha said to Srebrov, and I'm going to say more or less what he said, "Vlado, this is not a job for you. You are very hot-headed." It is a term that is used when you want to describe a person who can't control his nerves and his temperament. And he added, "We have to count down the tensions with the Muslims and the Croats, the tensions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that is not a job for you."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So how far in advance of the meeting, the 12th of July, 1990, had the inner core of the new party decided that Dr. Karadzic was going to be its leader?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there in February. I was there in March, as I said. Then part of the month of April and May, I spent at the seaside, for health reasons. When I came back, there was a general consensus of the people whom I came across there, and especially a consensus of those people that I respected and appreciated. So we came to the conclusion that at this inaugural conference planned for St. Peter's Day, on the 12th of July, well, that we came to the conclusion that Radovan Karadzic had to be proposed as the chairman of the party. At that time, the SDA, the Muslim party, had already been founded, and the HDZ, the Croat party, had already been founded as well. So the Muslims and the Croats had already founded their own parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many people, approximately, attended this meeting on the 12th of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: There were some six to 7.000 people. The hall was -- in Skenderija was full, really full. Many respectable guests were there. I was one of the organisers, so I know who was invited and who was there. I know everything that happened on St. Peter's Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who -- Dr. Karadzic became the leader; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. By acclamation he was elected, as well as all the other members of the leadership. So he was elected the chairman of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were there any members of other ethnic groups who were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: You mean representatives of the parties, political parties, or you mean those people who were there in the audience?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that among an audience of several thousand people, you can have no idea what the ethnic background of those people were. I understand that. But prominent members of other ethnic groups who were in attendance, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Well, they were there because they were invited to come to that meeting. As for your remark that it is very difficult to assess out of so many thousands of people predominantly Serbs, how many Muslims and Croats Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were there, I can say that some of my friends came out of curiosity, to see what the Serbs were doing. But as far as your first question is concerned, the chairman of the Party of Democratic Action, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, accompanied by one person, and by chance I know the name of that person, because it is someone I grew up with. Then again, Mr. Zulfikar - I can't remember his last name now - who was the president of the Muslim Bosniak organisation, was there. There was also Mr. Muhamed Filipovic, who was a member of the Muslim Bosniak organisation. Mr. Micunovic was there, who was the chairman of the Serb Democratic Party from Serbia. He was one of the guests. Oh, yes, I remember. The person I spoke about was Adil Zulfikarpasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic was invited to make a speech; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he made a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were there, you heard the speech?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you remember him to say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I know exactly what he said, because I remember it well, simply because myself and a great number of other people present were very happy to hear that. Mr. Izetbegovic started to speak by saying that he was not born in Sarajevo, that he arrived to Sarajevo when he was about four or five years old and that he lived very near the town hall. He said that he was very happy to see that what used to be an empty political space of the Serb national entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina is finally being occupied. And he said that he was very happy that people like Radovan Karadzic were the leaders of that party, that he was hoping that it would be a political partner of great quality and wished the party to get many votes during the elections. He also said that Muslims in Yugoslavia became fully nationally affirmed that their national identity was fulfilled in Yugoslavia and they would at no cost accept that somebody takes them out of Yugoslavia. He added that Yugoslavia was their home country and that he was happy that the Serbs saw things in more or less the same way, and together with the Serbs, they wanted to make Bosnia and Herzegovina a prosperous country within Yugoslavia. His speech lasted for some ten minutes, and it was interrupted on four or five occasions with huge applause of the Serbs that were present in the hall. He also mentioned a detail, that is, that in 1914, when Gavrilo Princip killed Ferdinand in Sarajevo, that his grandfather, who was from Bosanski Samac, the town where Mr. Izetbegovic was born, when they started to, in 1914, to arrest some Serbs, that he came in front of the policeman and said, "Take me together with my Serb brothers." And then there was a standing ovation which was almost as much as the one received by Jovan Raskovic, who was the SDS president for the Krajina, and he was really liked by the Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that speech, in case you think it's relevant information, a young man who was accompanying Izetbegovic, and I knew him, because we grew up together, he said, "Can you please accompany us through this enormous mass of people. There are so many Serbs we have to go through, because I am afraid for Mr. Izetbegovic's security." So I was leading the way, and then Mr. Izetbegovic came after me, and then after them, that young man. And the Serbs were split in two roads and allowed Mr. Izetbegovic to go to his car. That was a pro-Yugoslav - I wouldn't dare say that it was a pro-Serb - speech that he did at this inaugural convention of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think it's common knowledge that the party then established various organs and a way to run itself, and in particular, decided to have a Main Board and an Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that meeting, the Main Board was founded, and I was also elected to it, the same way as the chairman was elected by applause. Because at that time, the party was not ready for a secret ballot. We were not organisationally ready to proceed in such a way. We needed an initial period of time in order to see who was able to do what, and then to give particular tasks to different persons. So at that particular meeting, I was elected a member of the Main Board of the Serb Democratic Party. I think that some 50 to 60 people were members of the Main Board, and they came from all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A few months later, there were the first multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were not a candidate in those elections, were you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you involved in political campaigning?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Very little, because I had some family obligations, and also because of my work. I mostly organised things in the offices of the Serb Democratic Party. If you ask me whether I went to rallies and conventions, yes, I did go on only one occasion, but that was all before St. Peter's Day. I went to Doboj, where the initial committee had to be founded. And then they had to -- after that, there was a procedure. They had to found a municipal board and then they sent a representative to the conventions. I wasn't somebody who would go in the field and organise things in such a way. But on the election day - and again, it was Mr. Karadzic who asked me to do so - I was in the offices of the Serb Democratic Party. There we analysed the results. We had technical services. They were collecting information coming from the ground and I was the person who presented those results to Dr. Karadzic. Dr. Nikola Koljevic was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Main Board, from the 12th of July, 1990 to the 12th of July, 1991, can you remember how many times it met?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that with certainty, but what I remember is that in fact it wasn't really necessary. First of all, it was very expensive, and the party simply didn't have any money, any funds, to try and ask people from various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina to come there at their own cost, spend for petrol and leave their jobs for a day or two. Well, you understand what I mean. There must have been meetings, but I can't remember any particular decisions, any dramatic decisions that were taken at those meetings, because I had so many things to do with my work. But I know that between the elections and the month of September, I started doing other tasks. The meetings of the Board were more informative. Dr. Karadzic wanted to feel how the people were breathing, what they were thinking. He would tell them what he meant and then people from various regions would give him their opinions and their feelings, so that he could get a full impression of the party in the period that preceded the election and that prepared for the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were still in regular contact with Dr. Karadzic in the year that you were on the Main Board; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. But once again, not because of things concerning the Main Board but for other reasons. We would meet more or less every day and we would meet, for example, at the Holiday Inn hotel. Between July and the elections, the political council of the Serb Democratic Party was founded, and that was also one of the reasons why I would see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to come to that in one moment's time. Was Dr. Karadzic a well-organised person?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. He was a psychiatrist who wanted to hear everybody's opinion, and he lost too much time needlessly, to my mind, especially at those times, when quick action was needed. He spent a lot of time and lost a lot of time in discussions and assessments, and he was talking to people who delegated their problems to Dr. Karadzic. And they should have dealt with their problems in a different way. But you know, at that time, Serbs had -- felt that they needed to explain how things were going in their village to the chairman of the party. And in fact, he lost much of his time and energy in that. But he was not a type of man who was able to say, "Well, solve these things in a different way. Deal with them differently or with different people." And I think that needlessly he lost quite a lot of time in such conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned the political council of the party. Why was that body formed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Well, what I wanted to do in the first place was to get really top intellectuals. They wanted to include them in the political work. They wanted to have professors and doctors from various sciences. There must have been initiative of somebody from the Serb Democratic Party. What I wanted to do was to establish a body where top intellectual Serbs, Croats, and Muslims would be members, and they wanted that particular body to meet from time to time. They wanted them to be able to discuss things at that forum and meet occasionally and be able to get the impression of what the situation was like in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the original name was to be the Council for Inter-Democratic Cooperation. And the goal was to bridge the gaps between the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS, so the topmost -- or representatives or the more respected people from the three nationalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina had to form that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did the Council for Inter-Party Cooperation fail?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Well, simply because the Croats and the Muslims refused to take part in such a Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that council and the Serbs continued to think that such a body, an advisory body, wasn't necessary. But as the Croats and the Muslims did not want to take part in that body, the council was formed of members of only one nationality. So at the beginning, some 15 members, or the majority of these members, were not at all members of the SDS. Some kind of independent opinion of top intellectuals was what they looked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was your role within the council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I was invited by the party secretariat to come on that particular day, and I believe it was the 13th of September, 1990. So I was invited to go there, once again, with the friend that I had already mentioned, Bato Kecman. So I was invited to go to that meeting, which took place at the Holiday Inn. There I saw some people for the first time. Some of those people I heard of and I knew what they did, but I never had the occasion to meet them before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, there's one thing that is not entirely clear to me, which I would like the witness to clarify. That is, you told us that the parties started with the name not being the SDS because a reference to ethnicity or nationality was not allowed under the law at that time. We slowly moved now to the party being established and the political council of the party being, as far as I understand, an organ of that party. Is that a correct understanding? And when, then, did the party get the name SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure which party was set up first, the SDA or the HDZ. One of the two, anyway. But I'm quite certain that both of them were founded before the SDS. And immediately before naming the party as the Serb Democratic Party, I think that particular paragraph, that particular article in the existing legislation, was amended, and as of then, it was allowed for political parties to include ethnic or national indications. And I can't give you an exact date or an exact paragraph of the legal text, but I think that was the reason why we decided to call the party the Serb Democratic Party. And as to September, with regard to the political council, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to know whether the political council was an organ of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By inertia. Initially it had been planned as an inter-party body, and it was meant to have multi-ethnic membership. But due to inertia, as it were, it was turned into some kind of advisory body and then it was for the Serb Democratic Party, and afterwards it was made up of Serb intellectuals and academics only, doctors of science, professors, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the initiative was to establish an inter-party meeting place for intellectuals, and it later then became a place where only Serb intellectuals would meet, because the others were not participating. And then it slowly moved to the direction of a close relationship with the SDS. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Why did the others not want to participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not sure you in fact told us the job that you were given within the council. What was your role within it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: At that first meeting on the 13th of September, that is, that was the first time I met Professor Dr. Nikola Koljevic, who was elected as president of that council, and then Mr. Miroslav Toholj, who was a writer and poet, was his deputy. And I was elected secretary of that council. It was a job that was an unpaid position, and I didn't have the right to vote on any decisions, but I was in charge of organising meetings, booking meeting rooms, keeping records of the phone numbers, the names of members, and I was in charge of letting them know when the meetings would take place and so on. It was a clerical job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it's still not entirely clear to me. On that 13th of September, when you met for the first time, was that the old initiative, getting people together from all nationalities, ethnicities, or was that the stage after coming together from different backgrounds had shown to be a failure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said at the 13th of September, that is when the -- the first time you met, when Mr. Koljevic was elected as president of that council. You told us that the council developed from an inter-party, well, meeting place for intellectuals, into a party organ, more or less, at least closely related to the SDS. Now, at the 13th of September, was that the stage where you're still aiming for getting people from all backgrounds together, or was that at the stage where, as you said, due to inertia, this had failed and it had become a party organ rather than an inter-party organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer would be more in line with your second hypothesis. I myself was aware of the initiative, but all of us, until the last moment, were hoping -- at least I myself was hoping that when I entered the meeting room I would find the representatives of other ethnic groups there. I had not received the information that they had refused to come as yet. So when I arrived there, I only found the Serb representatives there, and later on I was told that they had actually rejected the idea of taking part. And so on the basis of inertia, it became a mono-ethnic body and became linked to the political structure of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also now do understand that the initiative to make it a multi-ethnic, that you're still hopeful on the morning of the 13th of September that by the end of the day the switch had been made. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How often did the council meet?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: In the beginning it was according to needs. Dr. Karadzic would let me know when the meeting was to take place and then I had to tell members where to meet and when. However, since it was a rather complicated way of proceeding, I think it was following an initiative from Dr. Koljevic -- no. Rather, let me correct what I've said before. It was Dr. Koljevic who was the president, who had informed me of the time and place for meetings, and he would arrange that with Dr. Karadzic in his free time, because Dr. Karadzic wanted to be present at those meetings in order to provide his point of view and in order to get some suggestions from members as well. But it turned out to be rather complicated from an organisational point of view only, and I think after the elections it all became properly defined. The meetings of the council would be held every Monday at 1800 hours at the premises that we were allocated after the multi-party elections. And that's the building of the American Embassy in Sarajevo today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And can you give us some general idea of the topics of conversation that were held within the council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The topic was always current political affairs during the week, from Monday to Monday. Everybody would tell about their point of view. They would suggest some solutions. And Dr. Karadzic, for the most part, tried to attend these meetings, unless he was held up elsewhere or had other duties to attend to. According to needs, we sometimes had other people attending meetings, following an invitation from the president of the council and following initiatives from members of the council. And they were invited to tell us about their work and about problems or incidents that they encountered. And if I may add: After the first multi-party elections, there was a shift in the work of the council. So Dr. Koljevic, in the period of time between September and the end of November, when the elections actually took place, and on that occasion, he was elected to the Presidency together with Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, who was also a member of the council. So since they were elected to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then we held another set of elections within the council. So the president was an academic, Professor Dr. Slavko Leovac. The new secretary was Dr. Sava Ceklic. And upon insistence, or following a proposal, rather, put forward by Mr. Leovac and Professor Koljevic, I became a fully-fledged member of that political council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what practical effect did that have for you, the fact that you had become a fully-fledged member of the council?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: It was a huge ego booster, you know. Whoever mixed with top intellectuals was respected. So it added to my feeling of self-worth, to be quite honest. But on a personal level, I had no benefit of any kind. I was very interested to hear about all the events taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was quite interesting to get those opinions first-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to now move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if you wouldn't mind, I have still some matters which -- it's just a matter of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Worthwhile dealing with now, Your Honour, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This initiative to create this body, first meeting scheduled for the 13th of September, was the invitation sent by all ethnicities or did you form a working group or was it an initiative which was with the signature of members of the SDS only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no invitations in that sense, I mean not a written invite. Immediately before that, I had heard of the initiative. I can't actually even remember whose idea it was, but I'm deeply convinced that it came from the Serb side. And I wasn't involved in the actual organisation of that first meeting. And then I've already told you what took place at that meeting. So I'm not in a position to answer. You are probably interested to find out why the Muslim and the Croat representatives did not attend. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find out how it could happen that there was such an initiative that already at its first meeting it turned into a body which was quite a different body what, as I understand, was in the minds of those who organised the meeting. So you couldn't give us any further information on how people were invited, whether there was any mixed group of supporting the initiative or that it was purely Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The annual conference, so to speak, of the SDS took place on the 12th of July, 1991, at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I was invited. I was invited as member of the Main Board at that time. And so I was duty-bound to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, did you stand again for election to the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But there was a secret ballot and I wasn't elected. So as of that day, the 12th of July, 1991, I was no longer a member of the Main Board. I wasn't re-elected. And by virtue of that, I was no longer Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a member of the Main Board of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is your theory as to why you failed to be re-elected to the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: It was a secret ballot when we elected both the president and the members of the Main Board. And I think that, according to the rules of procedure which were in place at the time, the president had the right to put forward a certain number of names of people who felt were worthy, on the basis of their activities so far, and also because of the need to get these people involved within the party. So it was at their discretion, as it were. They could put forward the names of certain people, in writing, and their names were included on the ballots. And I was on that list, and I feel -- I think that my lack of activity in the field, that I didn't go around, travel around Bosnia, et cetera, meant that people didn't know me, and they didn't feel like voting for people they had never heard of. And so they elected other people that they did know. And so it was all fully legal, properly done, et cetera. So it is in line with democratic traditions. I didn't get the sufficient number of votes, and so I was struck off the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as your place on the political council was concerned, was that affected by your failure to be re-elected to the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. These two things didn't overlap in any way, in the sense that I think you're asking me about. Not at all. My commitment and my work within the political council was totally separate from the Main Board of the Serb Democratic Party. This advisory council was an advisory body, as the name said, and they sometimes thought along different lines and voiced their opinions in different ways. And Mr. Karadzic and Mrs. Plavsic would listen to all that, and Mr. Nikola Koljevic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask about these elections on the 12th of July, 1991. How many people took part in that ballot? I mean, how many active members made up the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many more members of the party than members of the Main Board. It is about the rules of procedure. Not all members had the right to vote. But I can't give you the exact number. I can tell you roughly speaking what it was all about. I was entitled to vote as a member of the Main Board, and according to their positions, members of the Executive Board had the same right, the delegates from their local communities, local constituencies. I can't give you the exact number, but about a hundred people, perhaps a little bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the second question: Was the party already very well structured at that stage? In other words, did you have membership cards, membership fees? Was it a well and fully organised party? And in your view, how many people had joined the party? How many people were card-holders and had the possibly to actively engage in party activities at that stage? And we're talking about July 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did have cards. As to how many members we had, to be honest, I can't really tell. In my view -- well, I had never been very happy with the way in which the party was organised. Because it had never been a proper party, in the true sense of the word. Not a party, but rather a movement. They never managed to get it together, to get organised in order to have a good-quality technical service. Maybe it was due to the lack of funds. Because basically, it was a fairly poor party. I don't know how many members there were. But I do know what results were achieved at the elections. About 95 per cent of the Serb population saw that party as representing their interests, and they voted for them. So there was a broad-based support in the country. And as to party cards and membership, I really can't assess. And to be quite honest, I didn't even know at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The learned Judge, Judge Hanoteau, also asked about membership fees. Can you help about that at all, Mr. Divcic? Were there any membership fees, how much, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I really can't say much about that. I don't think there were any membership fees, and I think it was all based on voluntary contributions, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to move on now, please, to a different topic. You became involved in 1991 with an organisation called Dobrotvor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I think for the benefit of the note, because this is a word we're going to use a lot, perhaps I'll spell that. D-o-b-r-o-t-o-v-o-r [sic].

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should give the full name, and it is the Serb charity association, Dobrotvor. And it was a purely humanitarian organisation. Dobrotvor means charity. An initiative for the renewal of work. Why do I call it renewal? Because it was a very old organisation. It was first founded in 1917 only and exclusively as a charity, as a humanitarian organisation. And it worked until 1941, when the Second World War broke out. And in 1945, because of the system of government which was in place at the time, it ceased to operate. It was not banned, but it stopped functioning; it stopped operating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I don't know whether it's on the basis of your spelling, but what I have on paper is Dobrotvor, and that's how I hear it pronounced again and again. At the same time it's transcribed as Dobrotovor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without the second O.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was wrong. I'm very, very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. It's just for the record that we have the right spelling from now on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Though the witness was giving the history without my actually asking him, I was going to ask him the history of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So go on, please, Mr. Divcic. I think you were up to the fact that in 1945, it became obsolete, although it wasn't actually banned. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Go on, then, with its resurrection.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: This is why I used the word "renewing" or bringing it back to life, rather than starting to operate or to work. This initiative to bring the organisation back to life came from a gentleman who is in the clergy. But throughout its existence, it had strong links to the church. It was not the church organisation. It was not under the control of the Serb Orthodox Church. But many members were active clergymen. I heard of it for the first time from a clergyman in the Serb Orthodox Church, Vojislav Carkic. He worked at the Preobrazenska church at the centre of Sarajevo. After a religious service that we all attended, we gathered in the churchyard to talk a little bit, and I knew him personally through his brother as well, Mr. Tihomir, Professor Dr. Tihomir Carkic, who was also a member of the council. And we put forward this idea to Professor Dr. Nikola Koljevic. And he gave us his support in this respect. He felt that that would be a very useful idea, because he was familiar with the history of that organisation. And the Muslim Merhamet charity was already in existence, as well as Caritas, which was a Catholic charity. So once again, there was a void, in as far as the Serbs were concerned. So it was a Serb renewal, bringing this Serb charity back to life. And we had a founding convention. We were very active on that. Once again, we were in a quandary. We didn't know who to choose to lead the organisation. Because it was a big job, and we all had other duties. So all these were honorary duties, free of -- the work had to be done free of charge. And the first president, the proposal -- the first proposal was for Professor Dr. Slavko Leovac, but due to ill health, he couldn't accept. And so at that first convention at the end of November, and it took place at the Holiday Inn hotel once again, and so we elected a president and it was Dr. Andreja Gvozdzenovic, who was also president of the council, and I was his deputy, and I believe Mrs. Milica Koljevic, Professor Koljevic's wife. I think -- well, she had some organisational skills and she was interested in humanitarian work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And briefly at this point, because it's not terribly important: What was the role of the organisation in its infancy, that is, during its first six months or so?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Assistance to all those in need, no matter what their religion or ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll come back to Dobrotvor a little later. Perhaps I didn't ask you, just before we leave Dobrotvor: When was it that it was started up again? Date, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: You mean when the convention took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: It was the end of 1991, November or December. I can't tell you exactly. The end of 1991, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We all know that the political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina got rapidly worse in the early part of 1992. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would say in 1991 already, maybe not rapidly, but at least serious indications that a big difference is going to start for the SDA, and Mr. Izetbegovic, as the chairman of that party. Whereas with the Croats, the situation was really clear right from the start. If I may say so, in western Herzegovina, which is ethnically very compact, there are Croats there, it -- that there were discussions where they would join the motherland. And I know that Mr. Karadzic, at a meeting, those meetings mostly took part on Thursdays, so I was there, and what he said about it once was that, "I'm sorry that the Croats from Bosnia want to secede. We are against a split-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we are not going to fight about it if they want to secede." That I really remember him saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with your state of knowledge end of 1991/early 1992, so far as politics is concerned. You were still working full time as a telecommunications engineer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Up until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is my fault, in fact. I'm going to interrupt the flow of your evidence. I should have dealt with this before. I hadn't realised. You have in front of you a notebook full of notes that you've prepared for your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that at my request, those notes have been copied?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I can tell Your Honour that they've been provided by me to the Prosecution yesterday. I should have asked before the witness had begun. I completely forgot. They are trigger notes. He can describe to the Court how and when he prepared them. But perhaps I can just ask this one question. You prepared them for the purpose of your testimony here shortly before you were asked to come and testify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I was informed last Wednesday that if I would agree to it, on the following Saturday, I would have to come to The Hague to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am going to stop you. I think you -- the leading question I deliberately asked you and I think you can answer it yes or no. It's right you prepared those notes for the purpose of this testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The application is for him to be allowed to use them. As I say, a copy has been provided already, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... witness consults any written documents if the content is available to the Prosecution. If there's no objection against it, then the Court, who can't even see what the witness has in front of him, will not interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got a copy for the Court, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to hear the oral testimony. So as long as I do not hear from the Prosecution, I appreciate your sincere wish to be as open as possible, Mr. Josse, and let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you were -- what I wanted to ask you was your state of knowledge of events in late 1991/early 1992. You've told us a few moments ago that you were a telecommunications engineers up until April 1992. That's correct, isn't it? Did the political council continue to function up until the time that you left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I think that the last meeting of the political council took place somewhere towards the end of March 1992. After that, the conflict broke out and that body never met again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The meetings of the political council presumably provided you with quite a lot of political information as to what was going on at a high level within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Obviously, you had other sources of information, media, for example.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about your contact in that time, end of 1991/early 1992, with, firstly, Dr. Karadzic? How regularly were you speaking to him, seeing him, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you just repeat what period of time you mean, the year or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Late 1991/early 1992, before -- six months before you left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Mostly at the meetings of the political council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move on to your departure from Sarajevo. You mentioned this at the very beginning of your evidence, but I think it's worth your repeating it. Why did you leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Simply because I was scared. Serbs were really terribly scared that what had happened in the previous wars would not happen to them again. They were afraid of, if I use the term St. Bartholomew's Night, what would happen to them in such a case. We were aware of the fact that the Muslims and the Croats, and especially the Muslims, I have to say, that they had special units that were part of their political parties, namely, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. It was only after the war that we actually realised how dangerous that was. We know that at certain points in time they celebrated various kinds of commemorations, and at those occasions we saw that tens of thousands of armed units, or armed men, were present in units. So after the party was founded and before the elections, there was one of the reasons of the conflict between Mr. Srebrov and Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Srebrov insisted that the Serbs too need to have some kind of a militia. In his words, I quote him, he said, "We need to protect ourselves." So the conflict was dramatic, and Mr. Karadzic categorically refused that something like that be done within the Serb Democratic Party. We were of the opinion that, apart from the fact that it was illegal, that our political enemies would use it against us in order to arm themselves even better. We were really confident in the institutions of the system. We were confident that there was the JNA, and according to the constitution and to the law, it had to protect the sovereignty and the territorial integrity. We were also confident that the Ministry of the Interior would do its task. As time went by, the way I understood it, and I also discussed it with other people, I thought that that kind of protection might not be too strong and maybe we should not take it for granted. And that is why, on the 3rd of April, I believe, it was on the Friday, anyway, I sent my father -- we had a country-house slightly beyond Pale. It's some 25 kilometres away from Sarajevo. It's really a very small house, five metres by five metres, that I constructed in 1984. So my father left on the 3rd of April, with the children, and my mother and myself, we left after that, and we were not able to come back. All the roads were blocked. We were not able to go through. And by inertia, I stayed there and that's where I live today, and I work there as well. That is how I left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could I just seek clarification. You said your father left on the 3rd of April with the children. Is that with your children or with his children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a misunderstanding. What I said, he went by himself to prepare the house, to switch the heating on, because nobody had lived there for a long time, and I went with my mother and my two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was about to assist. Your Honour, perhaps I could ask one more question. I was about to deal with Mr. Divcic's family situation, which might clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd like to very much know when exactly he also left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before we turn to when you actually left, it's right that you were divorced from the mother of the two children at this time, in 1992? That's right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: No. We divorced in 1988. And the children, by the decision of the court, or rather, on the basis of an agreement between myself and their children [as interpreted] were in my custody. And so I was raising them, and I had the custody of my two-and-a-half-year-old son and four-and-a-half-year-old daughter. So I was a single father, so to say. I suppose that's the expression you use.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's exactly the point that I was trying to establish from you. And firstly, when was it that you left Sarajevo? What day?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of April, at around 11.00, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And were the children with you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. And my mother was with me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, your job, what happened about that, the job in Sarajevo, of course?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: I found out about that only when I was supposed to get another job at the electricity board at Pale, and so I had to compile my CV and show them where I'd worked before. And I got some friends to go and pick up my documents at my former place of work. And then I discovered that the paper said that my job contract at the electricity board in Sarajevo, which is my first job, and my father used to work there and he retired from that organisation, so the first day I worked there was the 1st of January, 1979, and apparently the last one was the 11th of April, 1992. There's no explanation on that document, but it was quite clear that I was dismissed because of my political convictions. But of course the formal reasons might also exist. For a few days, I didn't show up at work, for reasons that they were not told about. And I think that was the law at the time. If you didn't show up for work for a number of days and you never reported to anyone, you would automatically be fired. And I was prevented from going to work, and so my last day of work at the Sarajevo electricity board was the 11th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock. I said that we would stop today shortly after close to 1.00. Could you find a suitable moment within the next few minutes to finish for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next few minutes or the next 15 minutes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we started at -- I think it's 7 minutes past 11.00, so we are now in the second session a little bit more than one hour and a half. But not to stop the examination, but just for the day, within the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the home that you lived in in the village outside Pale was or is how far from Pale, in terms of kilometres, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: The house is three kilometres away from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you moved to this house, and we will call it Pale, had the Bosnian Serb leadership moved to Pale?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: No. As I told you, I wanted that my young children and my elderly parents be in security, much more security than in Sarajevo. I didn't want that anything would happen to them, and also I didn't want them to interfere if I needed to avoid some kind of problems. My intention was to go back to my flat in Sarajevo, but all the roads had been cut. In 30 years, I never heard of a road of which I heard at that time. It was a path leading through the woods. It was only some special machinery for work in the woods that was able to go through there. And the four-wheel drives as well. So at some stage I received information saying that Radovan Karadzic had arrived to Pale. So I went to see him. I greeted him and asked him, "What are we going to do now? Are we going back? How are we going to do things now?" He said, "To start with, we are going to stay here and get ourselves organised here." Later on, they started and dressed in a completely inappropriate way. It was early April, at an altitude between 800 and 1.000 metres. It was very cold then. And I saw that the people I knew, the doctors and professors, were coming in inappropriate clothes, those that they were wearing at the time. So I decided to offer help.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to stop you there for a moment. Could I just ask you: The conversation with Dr. Karadzic, are you able to date that, please? In other words, his arrival in Pale.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIVCIC
utterances.text: The 7th, the 8th, and the 9th of April. I can't tell you exactly. It was, anyway, about two, three, or four days after I had arrived there. That's my bearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm quite content to stop there, because I'm going to go on and deal in some detail with the arrival of the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given until now and you're still about to give, so no communication with anyone about your testimony, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, in this same courtroom. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could you give us an impression on -- it's not clearly in my mind for how much time this witness was scheduled, to give me an impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The question is how much longer I'm going to be with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would say about two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About two hours. Thank you very much. We'll resume tomorrow morning and -- yes, Mr. Josse. Is there anything you'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're just on your feet to be prepared to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's more that Your Honour looked at me, and when a judge looks at me, I like to jump to my feet to attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I'll be more careful not to look at everyone, because it ... We'll resume tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.
